name: The Scales of Ma'at
powers: Weighs the heart of the dead against the feather of truth in the judgment hall.
description: The great balance set up in the Hall of Two Truths (or Hall of Ma'at), where the heart of the dead was weighed against the feather of truth before Osiris, with Thoth recording the verdict and the devourer Ammit waiting to swallow any heart found heavier than the feather. Chapter 125 of the Book of the Dead describes the rite, in which the deceased recites the Negative Confession before the Forty-Two Judges. The scene, painted on tomb walls and funerary papyri from the New Kingdom onward, is among the most reproduced images of Egyptian religion. Because the heart (ib) was held to record the deeds of a life, its weighing decided the soul's fate: a heart in balance passed to the blessed afterlife, while one burdened by sin was consumed and ceased to exist. Modern exhibitions of Egyptian funerary art still make the weighing of the heart one of their centrepieces.

name: The Feather of Ma'at
powers: The counterweight of truth against which the heart of the dead is weighed.
description: The ostrich feather worn on the head of the goddess Ma'at, goddess of truth, order, and justice, and placed on the scales of judgment as the counterweight to the heart of the dead. A heart lighter than the feather passed on to the afterlife; a heavier one was devoured by Ammit. The feather, also worn by the god Shu in his role of lifting the sky, became the emblem of a life measured by truth. Ma'at herself is rarely shown without it, and the hieroglyph for the feather stands for her name and for the idea of justice itself. In later and modern thought it has become a byword for fair judgment, and the phrase 'feather of truth' is now used far beyond Egyptology.

name: The Golden Falcon of Hierakonpolis
powers: The earliest great image of the falcon god Horus.
description: The great gold head of the falcon god Horus found in the Main Deposit of the temple at Hierakonpolis (ancient Nekhen), the cult centre of Horus and one of the oldest religious and political capitals of Egypt. Made of beaten gold and fixed to a copper statue of a falcon, it is set with polished obsidian eyes and crowned with a twin-plumed headdress and a royal uraeus cobra on the brow. Long dated to about 3100 BCE and linked to the era of the Narmer Palette, which was found in the same cache, it is now more commonly assigned by scholars to the Old Kingdom, around the Sixth Dynasty (c. 2345-2181 BCE). Standing as a rare surviving cult statue of a deity, it shows the falcon god as patron of kingship, and a royal statuette once placed beneath its breast made visible the bond between the living pharaoh and his divine protector.

name: The Sistrum
powers: Its rattling pleased the goddess and drove away hostile powers.
description: A sacred rattle of looped bronze or copper rods strung across a frame, shaken in the cults of Hathor and Isis to please the goddess and to repel evil with its hissing, sibilant sound, called sesheshet in Egyptian after the noise it makes. Priestesses, queens, and kings bore it in temple ritual, and queens are depicted holding it in both hands; great ceremonial versions, often of gilt bronze, stood as temple furniture. Its naos-shaped variant carried the cow-eared head of Hathor between its handles and remained in use into Graeco-Roman Egypt, where it became an attribute of Isis in her universal form. The sistrum survives today as a liturgical instrument in Coptic Christianity and in Ethiopian Orthodox worship, making it one of the oldest sacred rattles still in continuous use.

name: The Crook and Flail
aliases: Shepherd's Crook and Flail of Osiris
material: Gold and blue faience (mythic and royal)
powers: Signs of kingship and of Osiris's shepherd-care over the people.
description: The crossed crook (heka) and flail (nekhakha) carried by Osiris as emblems of royal authority and of the shepherd's care for his flock, laid crossed over royal mummies in their coffins. Temple reliefs show the living pharaoh handing the pair to the god of the dead and receiving it back, and gilt and blue-faience examples were buried with kings such as Tutankhamun, whose tomb yielded several full sets. The crook descends from the shepherd's staff and the flail from the winnowing fan or cattle prod, and together they fix the enthroned image of Osiris that endured for three thousand years. In the Osiris myth the two signs, held by the dead god, tie the promise of the afterlife to the order of kingship that the pharaoh upheld on earth.

name: The Solar Barque of Ra
powers: Carries the sun across the sky by day and through the underworld by night.
description: The two celestial boats in which the sun god Ra sails: the day barque Mandjet crossing the sky and the night barque Mesektet crossing the Duat, the underworld, where the crew repel the serpent Apep with spears and enchantments so that dawn can return. The nightly battle myth inspired real solar barques buried beside temples and pyramids, most famously the dismantled cedar boat entombed beside the Great Pyramid at Giza, so that the king might make the same journey after death. The journey itself was written into the Pyramid Texts and the later Books of the Day and Night, which describe the gates and hours the barque must pass. Both the image of the sun sailing through the hours and the funeral barque that carries the dead echo through Egyptian art from the earliest dynasties to the Ptolemaic temples.
source: Pyramid Texts and solar barque burials

name: Ushabti Figurines
powers: Answer the summons to labor in the afterlife in place of the deceased.
description: Small mummiform figurines placed in Egyptian tombs to perform field labour for the dead in the afterlife, inscribed with spell 6 of the Book of the Dead, in which the figure answers 'here I am' when summoned to work in the fields of the god of the dead. A single burial could hold several hundred, from a modest clay set to the 413 ushabtis buried with Tutankhamun in faience, wood, and stone, each furnished with the tiny hoe and basket of the peasant. The name derives from the Egyptian word meaning 'answerer', and the figures were made from the Middle Kingdom to the Ptolemaic period, their form and text changing little across two thousand years. Overseer ushabtis, distinguished by a kilt and whip, were added in the New Kingdom to supervise the labouring rows. Today they are among the most common and most recognisable artefacts of Egyptian museum collections.
source: Book of the Dead, spell 6; tomb assemblages

name: The Djed Pillar
powers: Symbol of stability and of the backbone of Osiris.
description: The columnar sign shaped like a stylised tree trunk or a stack of ribs, symbol of stability and of Osiris, whose backbone it was said to be. Set up as a temple emblem and ritually raised by the king in the sed festival to renew his reign, it was also worn as an amulet of gold or faience to give the wearer firmness of life. In the Osiris myth, Isis and Nephthys restore the god beside the pillar, and the raising of the djed in the festival of Sokar re-enacted his resurrection each year. Countless faience djed amulets survive from graves, often strung with the tjet of Isis and the ankh as a protective triad, so that the sign remained a living token of stability from the Pyramid Texts well into Roman Egypt.

name: The Knot of Isis
powers: Guards the wearer through the power of Isis.
description: The looped red tjet amulet, the 'girdle of Isis', worn by the living and the dead for the goddess's protection and said to be her blood, her girdle, or the knot of her dress. Spell 156 of the Book of the Dead directs that it be made of red jasper and placed on the neck of the deceased so that the might of Isis would guard the throat and chest. Red carnelian and faience tjets are common in New Kingdom burials, where they sit with the djed and ankh in protective groupings, and the sign itself often accompanies the goddess in temple reliefs. As the girdle that Isis is said to have used to protect the infant Horus in the marshes, the amulet carried the mother-goddess's care into every grave where it was laid.
source: Book of the Dead, spell 156; amulet deposits

name: The Uraeus
powers: Spits fire against the king's enemies; guards the brow as the eye of Ra.
description: The rearing cobra worn on the brow of the pharaoh and of deities such as Ra, embodying the goddess Wadjet, protector of Lower Egypt and of the crown. The uraeus spat fire at the king's enemies and stood for the blazing eye that defended the sun god, and its image on the royal diadem made the king's anger divine. Golden examples survive on royal regalia, most famously the cobra and vulture that guard the brow of Tutankhamun's gold mask, the vulture being the goddess Nekhbet of Upper Egypt paired with Wadjet. In temple scenes the uraeus rises from the brows of gods and kings alike, and the 'uraeus serpent' became in Greek and Roman writers a byword for the power of the Egyptian crown.

name: The Senet Board
powers: Its play mirrored the soul's passage through the hazards of the afterlife.
description: The Egyptian board game of thirty squares in three rows of ten, played with five or seven counters and casting sticks or knucklebones, and the most common board game found in Egypt, in use from the Predynastic period to the Ptolemaic. The crossing of its hazardous squares mirrored the soul's journey through the afterlife, and vignettes in the Book of the Dead show the deceased playing senet against an unseen opponent to win passage into the next world. Boards ranged from simple scratched slabs to fine wooden boxes with drawers and playing pieces of faience and ivory; Tutankhamun's tomb alone held four complete sets. The game's funerary meaning grew so strong that senet scenes became a regular image of the tomb, yet it was also played for pleasure, with boards scratched into temple steps and pavements.
source: Excavated boards; Book of the Dead vignettes

name: The Palette of Narmer
powers: Ceremonial record of the king's victory and of the unification of the Two Lands.
description: A ceremonial siltstone palette from Hierakonpolis carved around 3100 BCE, showing King Narmer on one face smiting a captured enemy with a mace and on the other reviewing decapitated captives, long read as an early record of the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt. The falcon-god Horus perches above a bound foe on the same face, holding a rope, and the king wears the white crown of Upper Egypt on one side and the red crown of Lower Egypt on the other. Found in 1898 in the Main Deposit of the temple along with the golden falcon and the Narmer macehead, it is one of the most analysed objects of Egyptian archaeology. While modern scholars caution that its scenes may record a single victory rather than a whole unification, its grammar of the smiting king, the divine falcon, and the ceremonial palette set the visual language of pharaonic royal power for three thousand years.

name: The War Shield of Neith
powers: Emblem of the goddess of war and of weaving.
description: The emblem of the goddess Neith of Sais: a shield across which two crossed arrows are set, combining her natures as a war goddess and a weaver into a single sign. Attested as her writing from the earliest Egyptian hieroglyphs, the emblem was painted on her temple walls, carved on votive objects, and adopted as the badge of her cult city. The Greek and Roman writers Plutarch and Herodotus both describe the goddess and her warlike symbol, and Herodotus records the shrine of Neith at Sais with its festival of lamps. As one of the oldest goddess emblems of Egypt, the shield-and-arrows remained in use into the Graeco-Roman period, when Neith, identified with Athena, still bore the crossed arrows.
source: Neith emblem on early votives; Plutarch, De Iside

name: The Wesekh Collar
powers: Bestowed solar protection and divine favor on its wearer.
description: The broad beaded collar worn across the chest and shoulders by pharaohs, queens, nobles, and gods, built of rows of faience and semiprecious beads and capped with golden falcon-headed terminals, the name wesekh meaning 'broad'. Such collars were given as royal gifts, as the Amarna letters record the sending of broad collars of gold between courts, and they were buried with the dead, who are shown in tomb scenes receiving them from the gods. Tutankhamun's burial yielded dozens in gold, glass, carnelian, and turquoise-coloured faience, many laid directly on the mummy. The weight and splendour of the collar marked rank, and its spreading rays of beads lent the wearer the protection and favour of the sun god.

name: The Cup of Jamshid
powers: Reveals the whole world to the one who looks into it.
description: The cup of the legendary shah Jamshid, in which, according to Persian tradition, the whole world could be seen as in a mirror, so that nothing on earth or in the seven climes was hidden from the king, who used it in divination. Despite a common modern assumption, the cup does not appear in Ferdowsi's Shahnameh; it belongs to later literature, where it is also given to the Kayanid king Kay Khosrow, and it became a byword for far-seeing wisdom in the verses of Hafez and Attar. In later elaborations the cup was said to hold an elixir of immortality and to carry the seven rings of the heavens, and some described it as the 'cup of the seven planets' used like an astrolabe. Sufi poets read it as the purified heart that perceives divine truth, and in the twentieth century Allama Iqbal made it an image of the self that cannot be known from outside. Its ties to the older idea of the king's divine glory, the xvaranah, are debated by scholars.

name: Rostam's Spear
powers: The heavy lance carried beside the mace and lasso in the hero's trials.
description: The heavy war-spear (nezeh) of the hero Rostam in the Shahnameh, carried alongside his bull-headed mace and his lasso (kamand) through the Haft Khan, the seven trials, and the wars against Turan, and used to strike down champions in single combat. In Ferdowsi's epic it is one of the enormous plain weapons that suit Rostam's strength, and it is with such arms that he takes the field in the duels against the Turanian heroes and in the fateful, unrecognised fight with his own son Sohrab. The epic seldom dwells on the spear's forging, so its particulars follow the conventions of Persian heroic poetry rather than any single description. In the later Iranian imagination, Rostam's whole war gear, spear, mace, and lasso alike, became part of the fixed image of the hero, shown across the centuries in miniature painting.

name: The Feather of the Simurgh
powers: Burned as a signal, its smoke summons the great bird to help.
description: The feather given by the great bird Simurgh to the abandoned prince Zal and later to his son Rostam, to be burned whenever they needed the bird's aid, at whose smoke Simurgh came flying from Mount Alborz. In the Shahnameh the feather carries the infant Zal to safety when he is cast out for his white hair, and in Rostam's direst need, when the hero lies bound and helpless in a pit, the burning feather summons Simurgh, who teaches him how to escape. The gesture became so fixed that the burning of a simurgh feather is a standing motif of Persian heroic poetry. In later Sufi writing it became an emblem of the soul's reliance on divine help, the feather a sign that even the greatest hero must call on a power greater than himself.

name: The Mace of Faridun
maker: Forged for the young prince Faridun
powers: Struck down the tyrant Zahhak and freed Iran from his reign.
description: The bull-headed mace (gurz) forged to the measure of the young prince Faridun, which Ferdowsi describes being made before his campaign against the tyrant Zahhak, so that only his hand could wield it. With it Faridun struck Zahhak's crowned head and split the serpents that had grown on the tyrant's shoulders, ending a thousand years of unjust rule and binding the defeated Zahhak in a cavern of Mount Damavand, where he is said to be chained to this day. The mace, in its bull-headed form, links the hero to the cattle-rearing world of the old Iranian kings and stands in the epic as the plain, honest weapon that overcomes sorcery. It became the archetypal weapon of Persian hero-kings, echoed in the bull-headed mace that later poets give to Rostam.

name: The Derafsh Kaviani
material: Leather apron, gold, silk, jewels (later ornament)
maker: Kaveh the blacksmith; ornamented under Faridun
powers: Royal standard of Iran, carried before the shahs as a sign of popular revolt and kingship.
description: The leather apron of the blacksmith Kaveh, raised on a spear when he led the people of Iran against the tyrant Zahhak after the tyrant had devoured his children; the new king Faridun then adorned it with gold, silk, and jewels, and it became the royal standard of the Shahs under the name Derafsh Kaviani. In the Shahnameh, Kaveh refuses the tyrant's bribes and carries his apron to Faridun, and the banner, embellished with a four-pointed star and streamers, was said to have been borne before Iranian armies into the Islamic period. The story is retold each Newroz as a symbol of popular revolt and rightful rule. Scholars note that the apron-banner is a literary invention of the epic tradition, yet the name and the image of the blacksmith's standard remained so potent that later dynasties claimed to carry the true Derafsh.

name: The Belt of Tahmineh
powers: Binds the bond between the lady of Samangan and the hero Rostam.
description: A belt said in some tellings of the story to have been woven by Tahmineh of Samangan, mother of Sohrab, and given to the hero Rostam on the night of their meeting, binding their union. The motif varies sharply across recensions of the Shahnameh and in modern retellings, and Ferdowsi's own text describes no single canonical belt, so the object's particulars rest on later tradition rather than on the epic's lines. In some versions Tahmineh also binds a token, a jewel or an armlet, on Sohrab so that the boy might one day know his father, and it is this token that drives the tragedy when father and son meet unknowing on the battlefield. The belt is therefore best read as a romantic elaboration of the episode, invented to give the doomed pair a visible bond, and any account of it must be marked as uncertain.

name: The Arrow of Arash
powers: Its single flight fixed the boundary between Iran and Turan.
description: The arrow shot by Arash the archer from the summit of Mount Damavand to fix the frontier between Iran and Turan, a flight said to have been blessed by the giving of his own strength, so that his body wasted as the arrow flew. Reaching the far bank of the Oxus at noon, the arrow ended the war between the two kingdoms and fixed the boundary for the people of Iran. The story is known from Avestan references and from Ferdowsi and other Persian sources, and the arrow's course, hundreds of miles from the Elburz peaks to the Amu Darya, has been endlessly debated and romanticised. The twentieth-century poem 'Arash the Bowmaker' by Siavash Kasrai revived the tale as a symbol of national sacrifice, and the ancient festival of Tirgan still honours the shot.

name: The Seal of Solomon
material: Gold ring set with a stone (mythic)
powers: By its engraving of the divine Name, its bearer commanded the winds, beasts, and jinn.
description: The signet ring of the prophet-king Solomon, engraved with the divine Name, by whose power he commanded the winds, the beasts, and the jinn in Jewish and Islamic tradition alike, told in the Quran, the midrash, and the Thousand and One Nights. The midrash adds the ordeal of its theft, when the jinn Sakhr stole the ring and ruled in Solomon's likeness for forty days until the king won it back and hurled the impostor into the sea. Its seal, often drawn as a six-pointed star or a pentagram, later became a widespread protective emblem across the Middle East, North Africa, and Europe, known in Islamic amulets as the khatam Sulayman. The name, transferred to the star pattern, still marks talismans and jewellery from Morocco to India, and the ring remains the archetype of the seal that gives its bearer command over spirits.
source: Quran; midrash; Thousand and One Nights

name: Solomon's Flying Carpet
powers: Carried the king, his throne, and his court through the air on the wind.
description: The carpet of Solomon, woven of silk and green stuff, said in Islamic tradition to be large enough to bear the king, his throne, and his whole court, carried through the air by the wind at his command and shaded from the sun by a flock of birds overhead. The Quran records the wind as made subject to Solomon, so that it carried his vessel at his bidding, and later commentators and storytellers, among them al-Tabari, al-Kisa'i, and the Thousand and One Nights, expanded this into the famous flying carpet. The details, its size, its crew of men and jinn, and the birds that formed its canopy, grow with each telling, and the carpet itself never appears as a physical relic. In the West it became, together with the genie's lamp, one of the two signature marvels of oriental legend, though its developed form belongs to Islamic exegesis rather than to any single book.
source: Quran; al-Tabari; al-Kisa'i; Thousand and One Nights

name: Aladdin's Lamp
powers: Rubbed, it summoned a powerful jinni who granted its holder's wishes.
description: The lamp of the tale of Aladdin, added to the Thousand and One Nights by Antoine Galland from the oral telling of the Syrian storyteller Hanna Diyab and first printed around 1709. Rubbing it summoned a powerful jinni who granted its holder's wishes, while its twin, the old magician's lamp, drove the plot's theft and recovery, exchanged by the sorcerer for new lamps. No medieval Arabic original of the tale survives, so the lamp is a literary invention of the folk tradition, set, like the story, in China while speaking a Syrian idiom. The image of the rubbed lamp and its wish-granting servant became one of the most widely known of all magical objects, carried into every later retelling and adaptation from pantomime to film, and its shape still means 'genie' in world popular culture.

name: The Magic Carpet of the Nights
powers: Bore its riders through the air to distant lands.
description: The flying carpet of the Thousand and One Nights cycle and of later oriental folklore, a woven rug that carried its riders through the air to far-off countries. Within the Nights corpus itself the carpet appears chiefly in the later tales, where Prince Husayn buys a magic carpet that bears its master wherever he wishes to go, and much of its modern fame comes from European retellings rather than from the medieval Arabic text. Its details vary widely from one telling to another, some giving it as a plain travelling rug, others as a king-sized carpet with a full retinue. The carpet's fame grew so far beyond its sources that the flying carpet, together with the lamp of Aladdin, became the signature prop of the Arabian Nights in world culture, endlessly redrawn and refilmed.

name: The Bottle of the Ifrit
powers: Held a vast ifrit imprisoned for centuries until a fisherman freed him.
description: The sealed copper bottle cast up in the fisherman's net in the Thousand and One Nights tale of the Fisherman and the Jinni, from which a vast ifrit escaped in a pillar of smoke and, furious at his long imprisonment, threatened to kill the man who had freed him. The fisherman saved himself by doubting that so great a being could fit into so small a vessel, tricking the spirit back through its narrow mouth and sealing the bottle once more. In the tale the jar carries the seal of Solomon, whose name had trapped the ifrit in the deep for hundreds of years, and it is the loss of that power that lets the spirit out. The vessel became the archetype of the bottled-jinn motif in world folklore, echoed in every story of a spirit, demon, or giant confined by a magician's seal and released by the unwary.
source: Thousand and One Nights, The Fisherman and the Jinni

name: Sefer Yetzirah
maker: Tradition attributes it to the patriarch Abraham
powers: Describes the creation of the world through the Hebrew letters and the ten sefirot.
description: The earliest surviving Hebrew text of Jewish mysticism, the 'Book of Formation', which describes how the world was created through the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet and the ten sefirot, and sets out paths by which the mystic may emulate that act. Its opening lines attribute it to the patriarch Abraham, though scholars date its present form to roughly the second to the sixth century CE, and it circulated in short and long recensions. The text maps the letters and the sefirot onto the cosmos, the year, and the human body, presenting creation as an act of speech and counting. It shaped the whole later development of Kabbalah, whose language of sefirot and letter-mysticism grows directly from it, and it remained a living book of contemplation, even of reported magical practice, for centuries.

name: The Temple Menorah
powers: The seven-branched lampstand kept alight in the sanctuary.
description: The seven-branched golden lampstand of the Tabernacle and later of the Jerusalem Temple, prescribed in the Book of Exodus as a beaten-gold work with almond-shaped cups, knobs, and blossoms, kept burning in the sanctuary before the veil. Carried by the Levites in the wilderness and set in the Temple built by Solomon, it was among the vessels plundered when the Temple fell; its image survives on the Arch of Titus in Rome, where Roman soldiers are shown bearing it off. The fate of the lampstand after 70 CE, whether lost at sea, hidden, or carried to Rome and later to Constantinople or Carthage, became a theme of Jewish legend and diaspora memory. The seven-branched form, the most enduring symbol of the Temple, was adopted in the modern era as the emblem of the State of Israel.
source: Book of Exodus; Arch of Titus relief

name: The Ark of the Covenant
powers: Carried before Israel and kept in the Holy of Holies as the throne of God's presence.
description: The gilded chest built at Sinai to hold the stone tablets of the Ten Commandments, carried before the Israelites in the wilderness and kept in the Holy of Holies of the Jerusalem Temple, where it stood as the throne of God's presence. According to the biblical books it was made of acacia wood overlaid with gold, topped by a mercy seat between two cherubim, and it was borne on poles by the Levites; its presence was held to go before Israel in battle, as at the fall of Jericho. Legend holds that it was hidden away before the Babylonian destruction of the Temple, while Ethiopian tradition claims that it rests today in the Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion at Aksum. No archaeological witness survives, so all descriptions depend on the biblical text, yet the Ark remains one of the most enduring images of sacred kingship and covenant in world culture.

name: The Brazen Serpent
powers: Healed the Israelites bitten by desert serpents when they looked upon it.
description: The bronze serpent made by Moses at God's command to heal the Israelites bitten by serpents in the wilderness, raised on a pole so that the stricken who looked upon it lived, as told in the Book of Numbers. Kept for centuries in the Jerusalem Temple, it was later destroyed by King Hezekiah as an idol under the name Nehushtan, when the people had come to burn incense to it. Its story is told in Numbers and in 2 Kings, and the object itself is known only from scripture, with no archaeological trace. In later tradition the brazen serpent became a type of healing lifted up for all to see, and Christian exegesis read it as a foreshadowing of the cross, a reading that has kept the image alive in religious art for two thousand years.

name: The Sword of Goliath
powers: The heavy blade of the Philistine champion, kept as a relic at Nob.
description: The sword of the Philistine champion Goliath, taken as spoil after the shepherd David slew him and later kept wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod at the sanctuary of Nob, where the fugitive David received it, saying there was none like it. The weapon is described in the First Book of Samuel, and David's possession of it anchors his kingship narrative in the biblical account, the champion's own blade becoming the king's trusted arm. The Philistine forging of iron in the early Iron Age made such swords prized and rare, which lends the story its realistic edge. Its fate after the reign of David is not recorded, so the sword survives only in the text, yet it remains one of the most famous spoils of war in biblical literature.

name: The Khamsa
powers: Deflects the evil eye and brings blessing to its bearer.
description: The open-hand amulet of the Maghreb and the wider Middle East, called the Hand of Fatima after the Prophet's daughter in Muslim usage and the Hand of Miriam in Jewish usage, hung in homes, worn as jewelry, and painted on doorways, cradles, and vehicles against the evil eye. The silver khamsa was the standard talisman of North African Jews and Muslims alike, made in every register from plain sheet silver to fine filigree set with coral and enamel. The open palm, shared with the wider Mediterranean hand-amulet tradition, reaches back to Punic and ancient Near Eastern hands of blessing, so the form carries an ancient root beneath its later name. Today the khamsa has crossed into global fashion as a pendant and charm, while its protective use continues undiminished in the societies that gave it its name.

name: The Gris-gris
maker: Fqih (learned man) who wrote the contents
powers: Protects, heals, or brings luck by the written words sealed inside.
description: A small leather pouch worn on the body, holding written Qur'anic verses, prayers, or magic squares, used across North Africa to protect, heal, or bring fortune, known in the Maghreb as a hirz. In Morocco the hirz was stitched shut by a fqih, a learned man, who wrote the contents in ink, and it was worn at the neck, arm, or belt, its power resting entirely on the writing sealed inside. The same pouch-and-writing custom appears from Senegal to the Sudan under other names, and the French term gris-gris, of uncertain origin, became the colonial-era label for the whole family of talismans. The practice is documented in ethnographic surveys of Maghrebi folk religion and survives today, adapted to modern materials but still stitched and worn as before.
source: Ethnographic surveys of Maghrebi folk practice

name: The Tunisian Fibula
powers: Fastened the shawl and served as a bridal heirloom and protective talisman.
description: The large silver pin or brooch, often triangular with a central coral or enamel stud and a long pointed pin, worn by Amazigh women across Tunisia, Algeria, and Morocco to fasten the shawl, and passed down as a bridal heirloom and protective talisman. Known as a tazabt in Tamazight, it is among the most characteristic ornaments of Maghrebi dress, its shape echoing the Roman-era brooches that secured the cloaks of the same region. The fibula often held a chain linking a pair of brooches across the chest, and its pointed pin served as a weapon, a tool, and a token of married standing. Silver and coral remain the preferred materials, and museum collections of Maghrebi dress and jewellery display the fibula as a defining piece of Amazigh identity, still worn at weddings and festivals.

name: The Sword of Antar
powers: The great blade of the warrior-poet, wielded in his duels and tribal wars.
description: The sword Dhami, the chosen blade of Antarah ibn Shaddad, the pre-Islamic warrior-poet of the Arabian Peninsula whose exploits fill the medieval romance Sirah 'Antar. In the sira, Antar wins the sword in combat and carries it through the wars of the tribe of Abs and his long struggle to marry his cousin Abla, who appears in his poetry and in the romance as his lifelong beloved. The romance is literary, built up over centuries around the historical sixth-century poet, and the sword's named exploits grow with the telling, so that Dhami accrues its own mini-legend inside the larger epic. It stands alongside the legendary blades of Arabic tradition as the emblem of a hero who won his freedom and his name by the sword and the ode together.

name: The Jambiya
powers: Symbol of honor and manhood; drawn in the bara' dance.
description: The short curved dagger with a broad double-edged blade worn at the belt by Yemeni men, a symbol of honor and manhood carried from youth and drawn in the bara', the ritual war dance of Yemen in which lines of dancers flourish their daggers to drumming and chant. Silver-sheathed jambiya hilts, some of rhino horn, are treasured heirlooms and marks of tribal and social standing, and a fine jambiya can be the most valuable thing a man owns. The wearing of the dagger, its angle at the belt, and the dance itself are all attested across Yemeni material culture and in the songs and poetry that surround them. Though the trade in rhino horn has been banned, the jambiya remains the national emblem of Yemen, worn in daily life and in the bara' as a living custom.
source: Yemeni material culture and ethnographic records

name: Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi
powers: Said to command the wind and fell whole fields of grass; one of the Three Sacred Treasures.
description: The legendary grass-cutting sword drawn from the tail of the eight-headed serpent Yamata no Orochi by the storm god Susanoo, who then offered it to his sister Amaterasu; it is the sword of the Three Sacred Treasures of the Japanese imperial regalia, with the mirror and the jewel. Its name, 'grass-cutter', recalls the later story of the hero Yamato Takeru, who escaped a burning field by using the blade to mow the grass and turn the fire back on his enemies. The sword is said to be kept at Atsuta Shrine in Nagoya, where it is guarded and almost never shown, and no one outside the shrine has verified its state. Alongside the mirror and the jewel it stands for the martial virtue of the imperial line and for the divine descent of the throne, as told in the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki.

name: Yata no Kagami
powers: Reflects truth and brilliance; part of the imperial regalia.
description: The Eight-Fold Mirror hung from a sacred sakaki tree outside the rock-cave in which the sun goddess Amaterasu had hidden, its brilliance luring her out to illuminate the world again, in the central myth of Japanese kingship. Revered at Ise Grand Shrine as the mirror of the Three Sacred Treasures, it is held to represent the sun goddess and, with the jewel and the sword, the imperial regalia; its polished face stands for truth and reflection in Shinto thought. The mirror, like the other treasures, is wrapped and kept from public view, so that all descriptions of it rest on the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki rather than on sight. Bronze mirrors from the Yayoi and Kofun periods, found in burials by the hundreds, show how old and how central the sacred mirror was to the culture that gave Amaterasu her tale.

name: Yasakani no Magatama
powers: Symbolizes benevolent fortune and the sovereign's right to rule.
description: The curved jade bead (magatama) dangled from the branch of the sacred sakaki tree beside the mirror that drew Amaterasu from her cave, and counted among the Three Sacred Treasures of Japan it symbolizes benevolent fortune and the sovereign's mandate to rule. The comma-shaped bead is far older than the myth, appearing in Jomon ornament and by the hundreds in Kofun-period tomb jewellery, where the huge jasper magatama found in the great burial mounds shows how much the form was treasured. The name Yasakani is explained in the chronicles as 'the jewel of Yasaka', a place-name tied to the shrine of Yasaka in Kyoto, though the identification is disputed. Together with the mirror and the sword, the magatama stands for the gentleness of the sovereign, one of the three treasures that together legitimise the imperial throne.

name: Shichishito
powers: None (honorific and ritual sword)
description: An iron sword with seven branch-like projections along its blade, dedicated at the Isonokami Shrine in Nara and recorded in the Nihon Shoki as a gift from the kingdom of Baekje to the Yamato court. Its long gold-inlaid inscription, which dates the sword to the mid-fourth century, describes offerings made to a sun deity and names the Baekje court that sent it, making it one of the oldest inscribed iron objects of Japan and a rare physical relic of early Korean-Japanese exchange. With its strange branched form it is not a practical weapon, and it is best understood as a ritual or ceremonial sword, kept for centuries as a shrine treasure. Today it is registered as a National Treasure of Japan and displayed only rarely, still guarded at the shrine that received it some sixteen hundred years ago.
